title: Is Titan Just a Dry Desert?
description:
What Would Happen If You Landed on Titan? (Seas of Liquid Gas) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T3cBBss1F60

Is Saturn's largest moon, Titan, just a dry desert? Not even close. While equatorial dunes stretch across Titan's surface, Cassini's radar swept across the north pole and uncovered a drowned coastline of bays and islands filled with liquid natural gas — methane and ethane. And far beneath Titan's icy crust, tens of kilometres down (about 55 to 80 kilometres below the icy ground), Cassini's gravity measurements revealed a second, hidden ocean of liquid water, likely mixed with salts and ammonia.

Sources: NASA Science, Titan Facts — flowing methane and ethane lakes and underground ocean of liquid water (likely mixed with salts and ammonia) 55 to 80 km below the icy crust (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/titan/facts/); Iess et al. (2012), Science — Cassini tidal gravity measurements consistent with a global subsurface ocean on Titan (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1219631); ESA Cassini-Huygens — several hundred hydrocarbon lakes and seas observed by Cassini (https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Cassini-Huygens/Titan_s_surface_organics_surpass_oil_reserves_on_Earth); NASA Science, Cassini-Huygens — Titan's three large north polar seas (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/cassini-huygens/).

Pictures: Original animated explainers alongside NASA/ESA/CSA/ASI/APL imagery, with AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.

social.hook: Titan's equator is lined with dunes, yet Cassini found seas of liquid natural gas at its north pole — and a hidden liquid water ocean deep beneath its ice.
social.question: If you could send a submarine to Titan, would you dive into its surface methane seas or drill down to its hidden water ocean?
social.alt: NASA Dragonfly rotorcraft on Saturn's moon Titan under golden skies, captioned TITAN'S 2 OCEANS?
